chunks: And Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn Ghazwan, from his father, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) performing Tawaf. A man from my brothers came to me and asked me to walk with him to attend to a need. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) noticed me and said, 'O Aban, who is this man?' I said, 'A man from your mawalis, he asked me to go with him to attend to his need.' He said, 'O Aban, break your Tawaf and go with him to attend to his need, and fulfill it for him.' I said, 'I have not yet completed my Tawaf.' He said, 'Count what you have circled and go with him to attend to his need.' I said, 'Even if it is an obligatory (Fard) Tawaf?' He said, 'Yes, even if it is an obligatory Tawaf.' He said, 'O Aban, do you know what the reward is for one who Tawaf around this House for a week?' I said, 'No, by Allah, I do not know.' He said, 'Six thousand good deeds are written for him, six thousand bad deeds are erased from him, and six thousand ranks are raised for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the reward for interrupting prayer or worship to help someone else in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) prioritizes *khidmah* (service to others) over the ritual continuity of *Tawaf*, instructing Aban to interrupt even an obligatory circumambulation to assist a companion. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly principle that social obligations and helping others can supersede individual acts of worship when the need is pressing, highlighting the spiritual merit of such interruption as equivalent to a full week of Tawaf.
